Neurology · published research

Neuroinflammation

In animal studies, 660-nm red-light PBM reduced hippocampal structural damage and cell death in an inflammatory rat model, and near-infrared treatment reduced glial markers in obese mice. No human treatment study was identified.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In animal studies, 660-nm red-light PBM reduced hippocampal structural damage and cell death in an inflammatory rat model, and near-infrared treatment reduced glial markers in obese mice. No human treatment study was identified.

Summary of the Evidence

The neuroinflammation category contains seven unique titles: five animal research publications and two systematic reviews. The animal work includes two mouse and three rat reports. One dissertation and a later journal article describe closely related near-infrared treatment in diet-induced obese mice and appear to represent the same research work, leaving fewer than five clearly independent experimental programs. The two reviews summarize animal studies and add no new cohorts.

Human and clinical evidence

No human treatment study of PBM for neuroinflammation was identified in this category. The evidence does not establish a clinical effect in a neurological disease or in people with an inflammatory diagnosis.

Animal evidence

Jung et al. tested 660-nm red-light PBM in rats challenged with lipopolysaccharide. Compared with the inflammatory model group, treated animals had less hippocampal structural damage and cell death (Jung et al. 2024). A mouse study in diet-induced obesity reported reduced glial activation and inflammatory markers after near-infrared treatment (Saieva and Taglialatela 2022). Other rat work measures memory, age-related inflammatory markers or vascular signaling. The two systematic reviews cover broader models and report changes in glial activation and cytokines, but these pooled laboratory findings do not add direct evidence for patient outcomes.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo publication was identified. Tissue and cell markers were measured within animal experiments.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The studies use local or transcranial red visible light and near-infrared light, including the 660-nm rat protocol and near-infrared mouse work. Models include endotoxin challenge, aging and diet-induced obesity. The source records do not provide one consistent power, exposure duration or schedule across studies. Treatment targets and disease triggers therefore differ, and no clinical dose can be inferred from the animal protocols.

Interpretation

The evidence supports PBM-related changes in inflammatory markers and tissue injury in selected rodent models. It does not show that people with neuroinflammation improve clinically. The repeated mouse research program, model variation and absence of human outcomes limit how broadly the laboratory findings can be applied.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for reducing neuroinflammation in people because the primary evidence is from animal models. Low within selected rodent models for changes in glial activation or inflammatory markers.
Publications and records7 unique titles

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Five animal publications report changes in inflammation-related measures, but one dissertation and its later journal paper appear to describe the same diet-induced-obesity mouse work. Two systematic reviews summarize broader animal conditions. Human treatment trials are absent, so a clinical study with functional outcomes and a clearly specified target and dose is needed.
